claim: CISSc are localized in the cytoplasm of Streptomyces coelicolor.
source: CIS from Streptomyces coelicolor (CISSc) are localized in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by cryo-electron tomography imaging showing free-floating particles in the cytoplasm.

claim: CISSc induce cell death under stress conditions.
source: Under stress, they induce cell death and impact the Streptomyces life cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from viability assays.

claim: CISSc contraction and function depend on CisA.
source: We show by cryo-electron tomography imaging and in vivo assays that CISSc contraction and function depend on CisA.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from cryoET and functional assays.

claim: CisA is a membrane protein with a cytoplasmic N-terminus.
source: Instead, our findings show that CisA is a membrane protein with a cytoplasmic N-terminus predicted to interact with CISSc components, thereby providing a possible mechanism for mediating CISSc recruitment to the membrane and subsequent firing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cellular fractionation experiments and topology assays.

claim: CisA is not part of the CISSc complex structure.
source: Using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, we provide an atomic model of the extended CISSc apparatus; however, CisA is not part of the complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and confirmed by the cryoEM structure determination.

claim: CIS function in multicellular bacteria is distinct from type VI secretion systems and extracellular CIS.
source: Our work shows that CIS function in multicellular bacteria is distinct from type VI secretion systems and extracellular CIS, and possibly evolved due to the role CISSc play in regulated cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study.

claim: CIS are evolutionarily and structurally related to contractile tails of bacteriophages.
source: CIS are evolutionarily and structurally related to contractile tails of bacteriophages and are comprised of core modules, including a baseplate, a contractile sheath, and an inner tube (Brackmann et al., 2017; Taylor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: CIS firing is triggered by a conformational change within the baseplate.
source: CIS firing is triggered by a conformational change within the baseplate (Taylor et al., 2016; Böck et al., 2017) and results in the contraction of the sheath, which in turn propels the inner tube along with the spike tip.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: T6SS are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane during assembly and firing.
source: T6SS are abundant among diderm bacteria and in some archaea, and they are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane during assembly and firing (Basler et al., 2012; Durand et al., 2015; Zachs et al., 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: eCIS are assembled as free-floating particles in the cytoplasm and subsequently released into the extracellular space upon lysis of the producer cell.
source: eCIS, on the other hand, are assembled as free-floating particles in the cytoplasm and are subsequently released into the extracellular space upon lysis of the producer cell (Xu et al., 2022; Shikuma et al., 2014; Hurst et al., 2007; Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Many Streptomyces genomes contain a class IId eCIS locus.
source: Notably, many Streptomyces genomes contain a class IId eCIS locus, a subtype that is structurally less well understood compared to other eCIS subtypes, such as 'antifeeding prophages' (AFPs) from Serratia, 'metamorphosis-associated contractile structures' (MACs) from Pseudoalteromonas luteoviolacea, AlgoCIS from A. machipongonensis or 'Photorhabdus virulence cassettes' (PVCs) from P. asymbiotica (Lin, 2024).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CISSc mediate a form of regulated cell death that influences the onset of sporulation and secondary metabolite production in response to exogenous stress.
source: Using Streptomyces coelicolor as a model organism, we and others previously demonstrated that S. coelicolor CIS (CISSc) mediate a form of regulated cell death, which influences the onset of sporulation and secondary metabolite production in response to exogenous stress and unknown cellular signals (Figure 1; Casu et al., 2023; Vladimirov et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SCO4242 (CisA) is conserved in the majority of Streptomyces species and other Actinomycete species that carry a type IId eCIS locus.
source: We and others recently noted an uncharacterized protein (Casu et al., 2023; Vladimirov et al., 2023), SCO4242, which is conserved in the majority of Streptomyces species and other Actinomycete species that carry a type IId eCIS locus (Chen et al., 2019; Geller et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations and reference to a figure showing protein alignment.

claim: SCO4242 is encoded just downstream of the baseplate components in the CISSc gene cluster.
source: Interestingly, SCO4242 is encoded just downstream of the baseplate components in the CISSc gene cluster, a location that usually encodes tail fibers from conventional eCIS (Xu et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2019; Desfosses et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Purified CISSc particles from the ΔcisA mutant show assemblies in the contracted conformation, similar to wild type.
source: Negative stain electron microscopy (EM) imaging of CISSc particles that were purified from ∆cisA mutant cells showed assemblies in the contracted conformation, similar to the CISSc particles purified from the wild type (WT; Figure 2a, b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by negative stain EM images.

claim: In intact wild-type hyphae, CISSc particles are consistently observed in their extended conformation.
source: We previously demonstrated that CISSc contraction correlates with the cellular integrity of S. coelicolor wild-type (WT) hyphae and showed that in intact hyphae, CISSc particles are consistently observed in their extended conformation in the cytoplasm, whereas in partially lysed hyphae, the ratio of extended to contracted particles is approximately 2:1, and dead hyphae only contain fully contracted CISSc assemblies (Casu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: cisA-deficient hyphae only contain CISSc particles in the extended conformation, irrespective of cellular integrity.
source: Interestingly, and in contrast to the WT and the complemented cisA mutant strain (Figure 2c, e), cisA-deficient hyphae only contained CISSc particles in the extended conformation, irrespective of the cellular integrity of the hyphae (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by cryoET images.

claim: The fully extended state of CISSc is 233 nm in length and 18 nm in diameter.
source: Moreover, our analysis consistently showed only two CISSc conformations in intact and dead hyphae, respectively: the fully extended state (233 nm in length, 18 nm in diameter, n=100 CISSc particles) and the fully contracted state (124 nm in length, 23 nm in diameter, n=100 CISSc particles).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on measurements from cryoET data.

claim: The fully contracted state of CISSc is 124 nm in length and 23 nm in diameter.
source: Moreover, our analysis consistently showed only two CISSc conformations in intact and dead hyphae, respectively: the fully extended state (233 nm in length, 18 nm in diameter, n=100 CISSc particles) and the fully contracted state (124 nm in length, 23 nm in diameter, n=100 CISSc particles).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on measurements from cryoET data.

claim: CISSc contraction is not a consequence of cell death and requires CisA in situ.
source: While hyphal cell death can be caused by a range of external or internal factors, our results demonstrate that CISSc contraction is not a consequence of cell death and requires CisA in situ.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the cryoET experiments.

claim: The S. coelicolor cis gene cluster consists of 19 predicted open reading frames.
source: The S. coelicolor cis gene cluster consists of 19 predicted open reading frames (accessions SCO4242-4260; Figure 3a), including genes with sequence similarities to potential CIS structural components (cis1-cis16), as well as additional genes of unknown functions (including cisA) (Casu et al., 2023; Vladimirov et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and reference to a figure.

claim: The cryoEM structure of CISSc represents the first high-resolution model of a CIS IId subtype.
source: The purified assemblies were subjected to single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) for structure determination (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), yielding the first high-resolution model of the CISSc in its extended conformation, which also presents the first example of a CIS IId subtype (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Extended CISSc particles share the conserved eCIS architecture, including cap, sheath tube, and baseplate modules.
source: Our model shows that extended CISSc particles share the conserved eCIS architecture, including the three core modules: cap, sheath tube, and baseplate (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the cryoEM structure.

claim: The baseplate and cap maps of CISSc reached resolutions of 3.5 and 3.4 Å, respectively.
source: The resulting maps of the baseplate and the cap reached resolutions of 3.5 and 3.4 Å, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the cryoEM reconstruction.

claim: The final model of CISSc comprises 783 polypeptide chains that assemble into a bullet-shaped particle measuring 268 nm in length.
source: The final model of CISSc comprises 783 polypeptide chains that assemble into a bullet-shaped particle measuring 268 nm in length (Figure 3b, c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the final cryoEM model.

claim: All analyzed CISSc particles were identical in length.
source: All analyzed particles were identical in length, consistent with our in situ data of extended CISSc particles in vegetative hyphae of WT S. coelicolor (Figure 2c–e).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on cryoEM and cryoET data.

claim: The tape measure protein gene is absent from the CISSc gene cluster.
source: The length of eCIS particles is often controlled by tape measure proteins (Rybakova et al., 2015). We note, however, that the corresponding gene is absent from the CISSc gene cluster.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The CISSc cap comprises one protein, Cis16, forming a C6-symmetrical complex.
source: This cap comprises one protein, Cis16, forming a C6-symmetrical complex that terminates the inner tube and sheath, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the cryoEM structure.

claim: The CISSc cap architecture resembles the cap complexes of PVC or Pyocin R2 CISs.
source: This minimal architecture resembles the cap complexes of PVC or Pyocin R2 CISs, but it is different from the more complex AlgoCIS from A. machipongonensis and AFP from S. entomophila (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Xu et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2019; Desfosses et al., 2019; Ge et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and reference to a figure.

claim: The CISSc sheath-tube module consists of 61 sheath layers and 60 tube layers.
source: We found that the module consists of 61 sheath layers (Cis2-L1–L61) and 60 tube layers (Cis1-L1-L60; Figure 3b, d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the cryoEM structure.

claim: The CISSc baseplate module comprises a heteromeric assembly of the proteins Cis1b/7/8/9/11/12.
source: The baseplate module comprises a heteromeric assembly of the proteins Cis1b/7/8/9/11/12 (Figure 3b, c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the cryoEM structure.

claim: The CISSc 'wedges' consist of two copies of Cis11 and one copy of Cis12.
source: Importantly, the CISSc 'wedges' consist of two copies of Cis11 and one copy of Cis12 (Figure 3f), resembling the baseplate of Pyocin R2(27).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the cryoEM structure.

claim: No structural components resembling tail fiber proteins were detected in CISSc.
source: Furthermore, we did not detect any structural components that resemble tail fiber proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the cryoEM structure.

claim: Nine encoded proteins from the CISSc gene cluster were present in the final cryoEM reconstruction.
source: Out of the 19 predicted open-reading frames in the CISSc gene cluster (Figure 3a), nine encoded proteins were present in the final reconstruction, for which all atomic models were built (Figure 3b, c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the cryoEM structure.

claim: No density for CisA was detected in the cryoEM model of CISSc.
source: However, we did not detect a density for CisA in our model, suggesting that CisA is not part of purified CISSc particles but may interact with them via a different mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the cryoEM structure.

claim: Mass spectrometry results indicate the absence of CisA peptides from purified CISSc particles.
source: This finding is also in agreement with mass spectrometry results, which indicate the absence of CisA peptides from purified CISSc particles (Figure 3—source data 1; Casu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting data and citation.

claim: CisA consists of a largely unstructured N-terminal region, a transmembrane segment, and a conserved C-terminal domain.
source: Bioinformatic analyses (Casu et al., 2023; Vladimirov et al., 2023) and structural modeling of CisA suggest that CisA consists of a largely unstructured N-terminal region, a transmembrane segment, and a conserved C-terminal domain (CTD) that shares structural similarity to periplasmic substrate-binding domains (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and reference to a figure.

claim: AlphaFold3 modeling predicts that CisA can oligomerize into a pentamer via the CTD.
source: Additional AlphaFold3 (Abramson et al., 2024) modeling using just the ordered C-terminus of CisA, including the transmembrane domain and the CTD (amino acids 285–468), predicts that CisA can oligomerize into a pentamer via the CTD (Figure 4b, c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation and reference to figures.

claim: CisA-mCherry fluorescence signal is consistently observed along the hyphal periphery, indicative of a membrane-associated protein.
source: Using fluorescence light microscopy, we consistently observed a CisA-mCherry fluorescence signal along the hyphal periphery, indicative of a membrane-associated protein (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by fluorescence microscopy images.

claim: CisA-3xFLAG co-sedimented with cell membranes in cellular fractionation experiments.
source: Our analysis confirmed that CisA-3xFLAG co-sedimented with cell membranes, while the cytoplasmic transcription factor WhiA could only be detected in the soluble protein fraction (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data.

claim: CisA is a bitopic protein with an N-terminus located in the cytoplasm and a C-terminus present in the periplasm.
source: The results of this assay confirmed that CisA is a bitopic protein with an N-terminus (amino acids 1–285) located in the cytoplasm and a C-terminus (amino acids 310–468) present in the periplasm of E. coli (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the dual phoA-lacZα reporter assay.

claim: CisA is comprised of a flexible cytoplasmic N-terminal domain and a periplasmic C-terminal domain that is predicted to facilitate CisA oligomerization.
source: Collectively, our results demonstrate that CisA is a membrane protein comprised of a flexible cytoplasmic N-terminal domain and a periplasmic C-terminal domain that is predicted to facilitate CisA oligomerization.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a summary of the CisA characterization experiments.

claim: The production of functional CISSc particles results in significantly reduced viability of Streptomyces hyphae exposed to exogenous stress.
source: We previously established a fluorescence-based assay to show that the production of functional CISSc particles results in a significantly reduced viability of Streptomyces hyphae exposed to exogenous stress, including treatment with the membrane-pore forming antibiotic nisin, UV radiation, or the protonophore carbonyl cyanide 3-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP; Casu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Without nisin stress, WT, ΔcisA, and complemented strains exhibited similar sfGFP/FM5-95 ratios, indicating no significant difference in viability.
source: Without nisin stress, all three strains exhibited a similar sfGFP/FM5-95 ratio, indicating no significant difference in viability (Figure 5a, c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The viability of WT was dramatically reduced in response to nisin stress.
source: As previously observed (Casu et al., 2023), the viability of the WT was dramatically reduced in response to nisin stress.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The viability of ΔcisA hyphae was unaffected by nisin stress and comparable to the viability of untreated cells.
source: In contrast, the viability of ΔcisA hyphae was unaffected by nisin stress and comparable to the viability of untreated cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The ΔcisA phenotype could be completely reversed by complementing the ΔcisA deletion in trans.
source: This phenotype could be completely reversed by complementing the ΔcisA deletion in trans (Figure 5b, d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: CisA is required for CISSc-mediated cell death in response to stress.
source: Thus, we conclude that CisA is required for CISSc-mediated cell death in response to stress.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the viability assays.

claim: The absence of functional CISSc impacted the timely differentiation of Streptomyces hyphae into chains of spores, resulting in accelerated cellular development and reduced secondary metabolite production.
source: Previous studies showed that the absence of functional CISSc impacted the timely differentiation of Streptomyces hyphae into chains of spores, resulting in accelerated cellular development and reduced secondary metabolite production (Casu et al., 2023; Vladimirov et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: ΔcisA mutant colonies sporulated markedly earlier than WT and complemented strains.
source: Importantly, unlike the WT and the ΔcisA/cisA+ strain, ΔcisA mutant colonies sporulated markedly earlier (+ hr).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by microscopy and CFU data.

claim: The ΔcisA mutant showed significantly reduced levels of actinorhodin production compared to WT and complemented mutant.
source: Compared to the WT and the complemented mutant strain (∆cisA/cisA+), the ΔcisA mutant showed significantly reduced levels of actinorhodin production (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by actinorhodin quantification data.

claim: The cellular function of CISSc in S. coelicolor depends on CisA, and its absence impacts the timely cellular and chemical differentiation of S. coelicolor hyphae.
source: Our data therefore supports the conclusion that the cellular function of CISSc in S. coelicolor depends on CisA, and its absence impacts the timely cellular and chemical differentiation of S. coelicolor hyphae.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the developmental and metabolite production assays.

claim: CisA is an essential membrane-associated factor that mediates the cellular function of CISSc particles in Streptomyces coelicolor.
source: Here, we identify CisA as an essential membrane-associated factor that mediates the cellular function of CISSc particles in Streptomyces coelicolor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: In the absence of CisA, CISSc particles are unable to contract in the cellular context.
source: In the absence of CisA, CISSc particles are unable to contract in the cellular context (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by cryoET data.

claim: The deletion of cisA decreases the induction of cell death upon stress, which in turn affects cellular development and secondary metabolite production.
source: Similar to a CISSc deletion or non-contractile mutant (Casu et al., 2023), the deletion of cisA decreases the induction of cell death upon stress, which in turn affects cellular development and secondary metabolite production (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation and reference to a figure.

claim: A conserved feature of all previously studied CIS is the requirement of the contractile apparatus to bind to a membrane before firing.
source: A conserved feature of all previously studied CIS is the requirement of the contractile apparatus to bind to a membrane before firing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as established knowledge.

claim: Intracellular CISSc particles from Streptomyces do not contain structural components that can directly bind to the host membrane.
source: Finally, and in contrast to the previously described CIS, we demonstrate that intracellular CISSc particles from Streptomyces do not contain structural components that can directly bind to the host membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the cryoEM structure.

claim: CisA is required to mediate an interaction of CISSc with the cytoplasmic membrane prior to firing.
source: Our data suggest that CisA is required to mediate an interaction of CISSc with the cytoplasmic membrane prior to firing (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed mechanism based on the data.

claim: AlphaFold2-Multimer analysis identified the baseplate component Cis11 as a significant hit and possible interaction partner of CisA.
source: Interestingly, this analysis identified the baseplate component Cis11 as a significant hit and possible interaction partner of CisA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b–e).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by computational modeling data.

claim: A protein-protein interaction between CisA and Cis11 would be consistent with the cryoEM structure, which shows a peripheral surface-exposed position of Cis11 in the baseplate complex.
source: Importantly, such a protein-protein interaction would be consistent with our cryoEM structure (Figure 3b–f), which shows a peripheral surface-exposed position of Cis11 in the baseplate complex of extended CISSc.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as support for the proposed CisA-Cis11 interaction.

claim: CisA peptides were detected in crude purifications of CISSc from nisin-stressed cells.
source: While we currently cannot exclude the possibility that the proposed CisA-Cis11 interaction involves an additional unknown factor, we did detect CisA peptides in crude purifications of CISSc from nisin-stressed cells (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Extended CISSc assemblies associated with the cytoplasmic membrane via their baseplate were rarely observed in WT cells.
source: In agreement with this idea, we rarely observed extended CISSc assemblies associated with the cytoplasmic membrane via their baseplate in WT cells (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by cryoET data.

claim: CisA may serve as a mediator for the interaction of CISSc with the cytoplasmic membrane and as a sensor and checkpoint for inducing cell death under specific stress conditions.
source: We further speculate that CisA may not only serve as a mediator for the interaction of CISSc with the cytoplasmic membrane but also as a sensor and checkpoint for inducing cell death under specific stress conditions or in response to cellular signals.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation based on the findings.

claim: The C-terminal CisA domain shares similarity with solute-binding protein domains.
source: Notably, protein structure searches with Foldseek (van Kempen et al., 2024) using just the conserved extra-cytoplasmic C-terminal CisA domain (amino acids 310–468) suggest that this domain shares similarity with solute-binding protein domains.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The C-terminal CisA domain could potentially be involved in directly or indirectly sensing stress signals.
source: Thus, the C-terminal CisA domain could potentially be involved in directly or indirectly sensing stress signals.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation based on structural similarity.

claim: Recognition or binding of a stress signal by monomeric CisA could trigger a conformational change that results in CisA oligomerization.
source: Recognition or binding of such a signal by monomeric CisA could trigger a conformational change that results in CisA oligomerization, which in turn could lead to an 'activated' CisA configuration that is primed to mediate the recruitment of CISSc assemblies to the cytoplasmic membrane, followed by firing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed mechanism.

claim: The lethal consequences of CISSc firing for the producing cell may have driven the evolution of a stepwise mechanism involving a checkpoint that prevents self-inflicted cell death by accidental firing.
source: It is conceivable that the lethal consequences of CISSc firing for the producing cell may have driven the evolution of a stepwise mechanism, involving a checkpoint that prevents self-inflicted cell death by accidental firing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation about evolutionary pressures.

claim: A stepwise mechanism would ensure that CISSc remain in a free-floating and safe state within the cytoplasm until a stress signal induces CisA-mediated CISSc contraction.
source: Such a stepwise mechanism would ensure that the CISSc remain in a free-floating and safe state within the cytoplasm until a stress signal induces CisA-mediated CISSc contraction.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation about the proposed mechanism.
